name: Guyliner / kohl

lead: Guyliner is eyeliner worn by men, and kohl, a soft dark powder, is among the oldest eye cosmetics, worn by Egyptian men and women of all classes. The payoff is stronger contrast around the eye, so the gaze looks darker, more intense and more defined.

The term became popular in the early 2000s emo scene. In appearance forums men's liner is discussed for a more intense or hunter-eyed look. No research was found on how liner changes perceived attractiveness in men.

paras: Dark pigment is placed along the lash line, which increases contrast and can make the eye look larger or more defined. Traditional kohl was made from stibnite or galena, while Western products generally use carbon or charcoal.

Studies since the early 1990s have found high lead levels in some kohl products, and lead exposure has been linked to anemia and developmental effects, though some research disputes the links. The FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and considers it unsafe, with import and sale in the US illegal. Western commercial eyeliners generally use other pigments.

angle.text: Men use eyeliner or kohl to make the eyes look darker and more intense, a visible change as soon as it is applied. The pigment raises contrast around the eye for a more defined gaze. The style runs from ancient Egyptian use to 2000s emo guyliner.

lead: Guyliner is eyeliner worn by men, and kohl is the soft, usually black eye cosmetic from which much of the practice descends. Both are used to define the eyes: Wikipedia describes liner as able to make eyes look wider or smaller, create winged or cat-eye shapes, and, when applied along the waterline (tight lining), make lashes look fuller and the eye frame darker [1][2]. In appearance forums, men's eyeliner is discussed as a way to give the eyes a darker, more intense look with more contrast between the lash line and the skin.

Traditional kohl was made by grinding stibnite (antimony sulfide), while many modern and homemade versions use galena (lead sulfide), and Western manufacturers generally use carbon or charcoal [3]. Egyptians of all social classes are reported to have worn it from about 3100 BCE, and the practice spread across North Africa, the Middle East, the Horn of Africa and South Asia [1][3].

The term guyliner became popular in the early 2000s emo scene, partly through members of Fall Out Boy and Panic! at the Disco [2][4]. Men's makeup has since moved well beyond that subculture: Wikipedia's article on cosmetics says the stigma around men wearing makeup in countries such as the United States has weakened and that men's use rose in the 21st century [5]. No studies on guyliner's effect on perceived attractiveness were found; the research that exists on kohl concerns lead content and is described below.

paras: Eyeliner is applied around the contours of the eyes to define them and create different aesthetic effects [2]. A wide variety of formulas exist, and traditional wax-based pencils are reported to contain about 20 components, with around half the weight made up of waxes and pigments such as black iron oxides, a little titanium dioxide and Prussian blue [1].

For men, the practical appeal described in fashion and forum discussion is subtlety or drama on demand: a thin smudged line along the upper lashes thickens the lash base, while heavier smoky application gives a more intense look. Looksmaxxing discussions tend to frame liner as a way to make the eye area look more defined, in the same family as brow grooming or lash tinting.

Wikipedia lists liquid, powder pencil, wax pencil, kohl, gel, cake, shimmer and felt-tip liners [2]. Liquid is opaque and applied with a fine brush for precise, sharp lines; wax pencils are the most common and cheapest form; kohl is a soft matte powder that smudges easily; gel is softer than kohl and applied with a brush; cake liner is dry until wetted and often used for graphic looks; shimmer comes in glitter finishes; and felt-tip liners are liquid liner in a marker with a brush tip [2].

Winged liner extends the upper line outward toward about halfway to the end of the eyebrow, cat-eye is a thicker wing running along both lash lines, and tight lining places pigment right at the waterline, for which waterproof formulas are preferred [2]. Permanent eyeliner is a cosmetic tattooing technique that deposits ink along the lids [2]. Harper's Bazaar is cited as recommending short strokes when applying [2].

Dark eye lines were used in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia; possible reasons include shielding skin from sun glare and, as some researchers speculate, warding off the evil eye [1][2]. Kohl was worn in Egypt from about 3100 BCE by people of all classes, and was initially thought to protect against eye ailments and harsh sunlight; the Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) describes kohl compounds as protective for the eyes [3]. Egyptians used black galena on the upper lids and green malachite on the lower ones, and heavily lined eyes appear in tomb art such as that of Nakht at Thebes [2][3].

Pharaoh Hatshepsut had servants grind charred frankincense into her kohl, the first recorded use of that resin, from frankincense brought back from an expedition to the Land of Punt around 1500 BCE [3]. Lead isotope analysis of Nubian sites at Debeira and Ashkeit (about 2300 to 1500 BCE) suggests Nubians also used and possibly made kohl, challenging the idea that it originated only in Egypt [3].

The English word kohl comes from the Arabic kuhl [3]. In India the equivalent kajal is traditionally made from lamp or ghee soot mixed with oils, sometimes with camphor or sandalwood, and is central to classical dances such as Bharatanatyam; in Pakistan and the wider subcontinent surma is usually made from galena or other minerals; in Somali and Horn of Africa communities it is called kuul [3]. In West Africa kohl is described as worn by both sexes and all ages at weddings, festivals and outings, and in the Horn of Africa it is used to cleanse the eyes, lengthen lashes and shield against the sun [3]. Mothers in Yemen applied it to infants, and in India dots of kajal are used to ward off the evil eye [3].

In the 1960s liquid liner produced thick black and white lines associated with the designer Mary Quant, and punk and goth fashion later adopted heavy liner for dark, dramatic effects [2]. Glam rock of the early 1970s was defined in part by the makeup and flamboyant clothing of its musicians: Marc Bolan's March 1971 Top of the Pops appearance in glitter is often cited as its start, and David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust persona from late 1971 incorporated professional makeup, helping normalise androgynous fashion [6]. Scholars quoted in that article called glam an offensive cultural emasculation, and punk partly reacted against its artifice [6].

Emo fashion of the 2000s featured skinny jeans, black eyeliner and tight band shirts, with the look becoming a large part of the scene's identity from about 2002 [7]. The term guyliner entered popular usage then, partly through Fall Out Boy and Panic! at the Disco [2]. The emo label drew a media backlash in the mid-2000s, and some bands, including Panic! at the Disco and My Chemical Romance, rejected it [7]. A history of the practice, Zahra Hankir's Eyeliner: A Cultural History (2023), is among the sources Wikipedia cites on the topic [2].

In appearance communities, eyeliner for men is discussed alongside other eye-area enhancements: defined lash lines for a more intense or hooded look, tight lining for denser-looking lashes, and subtle smudging to deepen eye contrast. The visual effect is the immediate point of the practice: it works the moment it is applied and washes off, in contrast with procedures such as eyelid surgery or canthoplasty. Forum threads were not available to characterise specific community attitudes in detail, but men's makeup more broadly has become more visible in the 21st century [5].

In the early 1990s studies found lead levels up to 84 percent in some commercial kohl samples; a 1998 study of kohl from Oman and a 2004 study of kohl from Cairo found galena in samples, and a later study of kohl made in Egypt and India found lead in about a third of samples while the rest contained amorphous carbon and other compounds [3]. Research on blood lead is mixed: some studies link kohl use to higher blood lead and others found no link [3]. Lead exposure is associated with anemia, developmental delay, lower IQ, convulsions and, in severe cases, death [3].

A 2016 Pakistani study of pregnant women's nails found 13 of 84 samples exceeded a lead concentration seen in a fatal poisoning case; the surma particles were in a respirable size range and about 5.2 percent of the lead was bioavailable in laboratory tests [3]. The US FDA does not list kohl among approved color additives and considers it unsafe, mainly because of potential lead content, and importing or selling it in the US is prohibited [3]. Wikipedia also reports a 2010 French laboratory study in which lead compounds from ancient Egyptian eye makeup raised nitric oxide production at very low concentrations, which the study's authors suggested might enhance immune response, and a test in which kohl inhibited some bacteria in the lab [3].

Western makeup eyeliners generally use carbon, iron oxides and other pigments rather than lead sulfide [1][3]. Non-lead products are sometimes considered inferior by traditional users, which the article says has kept up demand for handmade lead-based kohl [3].
No studies found on guyliner and appearance. Published research on kohl concerns lead content, blood lead levels and laboratory antimicrobial tests [3].

lore.intro: Claims about eyeliner and kohl circulate in appearance and cultural discussion: that liner changes how the eyes read, that kohl protects the eyes, and that traditional kohl is safe or unsafe. Positions below are drawn from encyclopedic accounts of traditional use and regulators.

claims.claim: Tight lining makes lashes look thicker and the eyes more intense.
Kohl protects the eyes from glare and disease.
Traditional lead-based kohl is not harmful and non-lead substitutes are inferior.
Lead in ancient Egyptian eye makeup gave immune benefits.
Men wearing eyeliner is a passing subculture or novelty.
